interest: This file is valuable to historians of interwar East Asia and World War II origins because it traces the transition of American monitoring of Japanese mineral resources from routine, peacetime statistical exchanges in the early 1930s to urgent military intelligence assessments by 1938. The earlier despatches illustrate routine bilateral statistical reporting and delays caused by Japanese bureaucratic backlogs, while the 1935 cross-reference sheets reveal Japanese diplomatic probing into Philippine natural resource concessions and strategic evaluations of Chinese raw materials. The 1938 G-2 report provides crucial granular evidence of Japan's severe metallic mineral shortages during the Second Sino-Japanese War, detailing the implementation of drastic state-directed conservation, compulsory acquisition of idle metal stocks, and nationwide domestic scrap salvage campaigns.
overview: This State Department decimal file (894.63) covers Japanese mines, mining, and mineral concessions between 1931 and 1938. The collection begins with diplomatic despatches from the American Consulate General in Tokyo explaining delays in and subsequently transmitting official 1930 mineral production statistics from the Japanese Ministry of Commerce and Industry to the U.S. Bureau of Mines. It also contains cross-reference sheets indexing State Department documentation regarding Japanese interest in reciprocal natural resource development rights in the Philippine Islands and comparative studies of Chinese and Japanese raw materials. The file concludes with a detailed 1938 U.S. Military Intelligence report on emergency Japanese government measures to conserve metallic minerals—including compulsory state purchases of idle stocks of iron, steel, and non-ferrous metals and nationwide scrap collection—to sustain key war industries and export production during the conflict in China.

subfiles.about: Explaining the delay in obtaining and submitting Japanese mineral production statistics for calendar year 1930 requested by the U.S. Bureau of Mines.
subfiles.from: Lee D. Sturgeon, American Consul in Charge, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Consul in Charge Lee D. Sturgeon reports to the Secretary of State that data requested by the U.S. Bureau of Mines regarding Japanese mineral production for 1930 will not be available until late 1931 or early 1932. He notes that a similar delay occurred with the previous report and attributes the backlog to delays in statistical compilation by Japanese government offices.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 180 on delay in securing 1930 Bureau of Mines questionnaires

subfiles.about: Transmitting official 1930 mineral production report forms obtained from the Japanese Department of Commerce and Industry for the U.S. Bureau of Mines.
subfiles.from: Arthur Garrels, American Consul General, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: American Consul General Arthur Garrels transmits completed questionnaires and report forms concerning mineral production in Japan for calendar year 1930 to the Secretary of State. The report notes that all figures are official, having been obtained from the Bureau of Mines of the Japanese Department of Commerce and Industry. Pages 2 through 4 comprise the original despatch and its duplicate filed copies.
subfiles.title: Despatch transmitting mineral report for the Bureau of Mines

subfiles.about: Cross-referencing a memorandum on the Japanese government's desire for reciprocal resource development privileges in Japan and the Philippine Islands.
subfiles.summary: This cross-reference sheet indexes a State Department memorandum by Eugene H. Dooman dated March 5, 1935, filed under Fw. 811b.011/10 and addressed to the Division of Far Eastern Affairs. The document concerns the Japanese Government's desire for reciprocal legal privileges under the laws of Japan and the Philippine Islands regarding the development of natural resources.
subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet: Japanese desire for reciprocal resource privileges in the Philippines

subfiles.about: Cross-referencing a study comparing Chinese and Japanese raw materials and their availability for Japanese industry.
subfiles.from: Nelson T. Johnson, American Legation/Embassy, China
subfiles.summary: This cross-reference sheet indexes report No. 3678 from Nelson T. Johnson in China, dated July 10, 1935, and filed under 793.94/7230. The referenced study examines China's and Japan's raw materials, comparing their variety, volume, and availability for use by domestic industry in Japan.
subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet: Study of Japan's and China's raw materials

subfiles.about: Reporting on Japanese government plans for the conservation, compulsory state purchase, and salvage of metallic minerals for wartime industry.
subfiles.from: Harry I. T. Creswell, Major and Military Attaché, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: U.S. Military Attaché Major Harry I. T. Creswell reports on measures undertaken by the Japanese government to tighten control over key metals including iron, steel, copper, nickel, lead, zinc, and tin. The government plans to purchase all idle metal stocks through joint sales companies and establish salvage firms to systematically collect household and industrial scrap metal. Major Creswell analyzes these developments as evidence of serious Japanese apprehension over strategic raw material supplies during the ongoing war in China.
subfiles.title: G-2 Report No. 9445/9545 on metallic mineral conservation plans
subfiles.to: Assistant Chief of Staff, G-2, War Department
